    {\huge\bfseries Abstract\par}

    \vspace{0.5cm}
    
    \begin{justify}
    
    {\normalsize The aim of this study is to identify which modelling framework and biomarker strategy provide the most accurate prediction of progression to Alzheimer’s disease dementia using longitudinal blood-based biomarkers. Phosphorylated tau-181 (p-tau181) and neurofilament light chain (NfL) are promising indicators of Alzheimer’s disease pathology and neurodegeneration, but their comparative and combined prognostic value across modelling approaches remains unclear. Using data from the ADNI cohort, predictive performance was evaluated across Cox proportional hazards (Cox PH) models, joint models (JMs), and joint latent class mixed models (JLCMMs), incorporating baseline and longitudinal biomarker information. Model performance was assessed using time-dependent discrimination and calibration across 1-5 year horizons. The results demonstrated that predictive accuracy varied across modelling frameworks and follow-up time, with joint models improving discrimination relative to Cox PH models, particularly at earlier horizons, while JLCMMs provided comparable or improved short-term calibration but no consistent overall superiority across time. Across all modelling approaches, combining p-tau181 and NfL consistently yielded the best predictive performance, while each biomarker alone showed similar but weaker performance, indicating complementary prognostic information. Consequently, this study may improve the understanding of optimal approaches for early disease prediction using blood-based biomarkers..\par}
    
    \end{justify}
    
    \vspace{0.5cm}
    
    {\normalsize Keywords: Alzheimer’s disease, dementia progression, blood-based biomarkers, p-tau181, neurofilament light chain, survival analysis\par}
