# Introduction

## Background

According to the World Health Organization (2025), Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disorder and a leading cause of dementia around the world with no definitive cure. The 2011 National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer’s Association (NIA-AA) diagnostic guidelines describe the disease as a continuum with three stages: a symptom-free stage (pre-clinical AD), a pre-dementia stage (mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to AD) and a dementia stage (dementia due to AD) (Carrillo et al. 2013, p. 596). Pathophysiological changes due to AD can begin up to 20 years before clinical symptoms appear, highlighting the crucial importance of early diagnosis and timely intervention to potentially slow the progression of the disease (Carrillo et al., p. 595).

In the context of AD, the term "biomarker" is commonly used and is defined as "a characteristic that is objectively measured and evaluated as an indicator of normal biological processes, pathogenic processes, or pharmacologic responses to a therapeutic intervention." (Biomarkers Definitions Working Group, 2001, p. 91).

AD pathophysiology has typically been detected by positron emission topography (PET) to confirm the presence and degree of amyloid plaques in the brain or by quantification of biomarkers implicated in AD pathology in cerbrospinal fluid (CSF) (Mattsson et al., 2017, p. 557). The former method involves radiation and the latter requires a lumbar puncture in order to extract the CSF, both of which are invasive procedures. WHO published a report in 2024 highlighting the promising progress made in recent years regarding the use of blood-based biomarkers to support AD diagnosis (WHO, p. 6). Specifically, recent breakthroughs in technology (Rissin et al., 2010) have allowed for quantification of biomarkers at much smaller concentrations than previous methods, typically being up to 1000 times more sensitive (Chang et al., 2012, p. 2). Using this method, biomarkers can be detected peripherally from their origin where concentrations are much smaller. These advances mean that the previously utilised invasive procedures can be substituted with easy to administer blood tests.

There are several core biomarkers used in the diagnosis and staging of AD (Jack et al., 2024), such as tau protein phosphorylated at the threonine-181 position (p-tau181), with concentrations expected to be higher in individuals with AD pathology (Wong et al., 2012, p. 815). Neurofilament light chain (NfL), a marker of neuronal injury not specific to AD (Jack et al., p. 5158), is also of importance. NfL is usually present inside neurons, and therefore concentrations are expected to be higher in individuals with neuronal injury symptomatic of AD (Clark et al., 2021, p. 7). Research suggests that NfL may be used as a prognostic marker of cognitive decline, supporting the diagnosis of a myriad of diseases including frontotemporal dementia, whilst p-tau181 is more useful for differentiating AD from other neurodegenerative conditions (WHO, 2024, p. 7).

These two blood-based biomarkers, along with various other biomarkers and clinical measures related to AD, are the focus of the *Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative* (ADNI), whose main goals are to provide open-access data to researchers worldwide and to improve the diagnosis of AD (ADNI, n.d.-a). Since 2004, researchers across more than 60 clinical sites in the USA and Canada have continuously collected and analyzed data throughout the different phases of the study. Blood samples from the ADNI cohort have been retrospectively analysed using the recently developed quantification method in order to measure p-tau181 and NfL concentrations (Zetterberg & Blennow, 2020; Blennow, 2018).

## Research Context

Recent research has applied a range of statistical models to biomarker data to predict progression to AD dementia and evaluate their predictive performance. For instance, a 2021 study fitted a Cox proportional hazards (Cox PH) model incorporating baseline values of p-tau181, alongside demographic and genetic covariates such as age, gender and apolipoprotein-$ε4$ (APOE-$ε4$) status. The study included a total of 767 participants from the ADNI database. Predictive performance was evaluated using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis at a fixed prediction horizon, yielding an Area Under the Curve (AUC) value of 0.78. This suggests that the model demonstrated good discriminative ability in identifying individuals who later developed AD dementia during follow-up (Wang et al., 2021, pp. 1-2).

Similarly, a large population-based study of 2,148 older adults in Sweden used a single multivariable Cox proportional hazards model with p-tau181 and NfL, along with other biomarkers, as baseline predictors to assess their predictive value for progression to all-cause and Alzheimer’s disease dementia. The model was additionally adjusted for age, sex, education, and relevant cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidities, as well as APOE-$ε4$ status. Predictive performance was assessed using a fixed 10-year prediction horizon, where the AUC was calculated based on dementia occurrence within 10 years. Within this framework, the presence of elevated values of one, two, or three biomarkers yielded AUC values of 0.74, 0.77, and 0.81 for AD dementia, respectively, demonstrating progressively improved discriminative ability for identifying individuals who subsequently developed AD dementia (Grande et al., 2025, pp. 2027-2031).

The joint modelling framework extends the Cox PH model by linking a longitudinal model which accounts for the effect of an endogenous time-dependent covariate measured with error, such as a biomarker (Rizopoulos, 2012, p. vii). This approach has been applied to model the relationship between repeated plasma p-tau181 and NfL measurements on the progression risk to AD in a cohort of 1191 participants, adjusted for age, gender, APOE-$ε4$ status and marital status. By evaluating AUC and Brier score at different time points and time spans, the researchers found that p-tau181 and NfL exhibited comparable performance in terms of both discriminative capability and predictive accuracy, with AUC values around 0.65 to 0.68 and Brier scores ranging from approximately 0.07 to 0.20 for the models. Additionally, they found that model incorporating biomarkers simultaneosuly showed improved performance, with slightly higher AUC values and lower Brier scores (Yuan et al., 2024, pp. 1, 4).

Furthermore, the simultaneous modelling of multivariate longitudinal biomarkers and clinical endpoints when heterogeneity is highly suspected has been handled by joint latent class mixed models (JLCMMs) (Proust-Lima et al., 2023, p. 3996). JLCMMs model complex disease progression whilst offering a method for the exploration of new pathological hypotheses and identification of subphenotypes. One application of a multi-dimensional JLCMM captured heterogeneity in the trajectories of three cognitive domains (memory, language, and executive functioning) from the time of Alzheimer’s dementia diagnosis (Scollard et al., 2026, p. 383). They identified five latent classes differentiated by overall level of impairment (low-high) and rate of decline (slow-fast). Within each latent class, the pattern of decline was relatively consistent across cognitive domains, suggesting parallel deterioration across functions rather than domain-specific divergence. In addition, class membership was associated with several key variables, such as APOE-$ε4$ status, gender, race, education and neuropathological burden (Scollard et al., 2026, p. 383). Despite these advances, such modelling approaches have rarely been applied to longitudinal blood-based biomarkers in AD research.

While the predictive performance of most of these modelling approaches has been examined separately, often using different datasets and under different data conditions, few studies have systematically compared them within a unified framework, particularly for blood-based biomarkers such as p-tau181 and NfL. Such comparisons have however been conducted in other domains. For instance, a 2025 study compared modelling approaches for mortality risk prediction in peritoneal dialysis patients, evaluating Cox PH models using baseline, time-averaged, and time-dependent biomarker values, as well as JMs (Goksuluk et al., 2025, pp. 1, 4-5). Overall, JMs demonstrated superior predictive performance based on AUC, with multivariate JMs performing slightly better than separate JMs fitted for each biomarker (Goksuluk et al., 2025, p. 8).

## Research Aims

This study investigates the prediction of progression to AD due to dementia (AD dementia) using longitudinal blood biomarker data, comparing traditional and advanced statistical modelling approaches, as well as different biomarker specifications. More specifically, the research questions are:

1.  What provides the best prediction of time to AD dementia: accounting for baseline biomarker values only, longitudinal biomarker trajectories, or longitudinal biomarker trajectories together with latent class structure?
2.  Across these modelling approaches, which biomarker strategy (NfL, p-tau181, or a combination of the biomarkers) provides the best prediction of time to AD dementia?

# Methodology

To address the research questions, a series of statistical models will be implemented. In all models, time to progression to AD dementia, defined as the first recorded diagnosis of dementia after baseline time, serves as the survival outcome. Given the relatively recent focus on blood-based biomarkers in AD research, their inclusion was considered timely and relevant. Blood-based p-tau181 and NfL were selected due to their established relevance for predicting dementia and AD progression, as well as the availability of rich longitudinal data with repeated measurements and overlapping follow-up information. In addition, they reflect two distinct pathological processes, making them suitable for comparative analyses of disease progression.

First, Cox PH models will be used to assess associations between baseline biomarker levels and progression risk. In these models, p-tau181 and NfL will be included either separately or jointly to allow comparison of their individual and combined effects. Second, JMs will be used to investigate how longitudinal biomarker trajectories are associated with the survival outcome. Initially, univariate JMs will be fitted for each biomarker separately. After that, multivariate JMs including both p-tau181 and NfL simultaneously will be applied to account for their combined and potentially correlated effects on disease progression. Finally, JLCMMs will be used to identify subgroups with distinct longitudinal biomarker trajectories and associated progression risks. As with the JM approach, both univariate and multivariate models will be evaluated.

All models will additionally be adjusted for baseline age, gender, and APOE-$ε4$ status to improve predictive accuracy. In the JMs, these covariates will be included in both submodels, as they are assumed to have direct effects on both the longitudinal trajectory and the time-to-event process, ensuring coherent and well-specified predictions across the joint model components. The significance level will be set at 0.05 for all analyses.

Subsequently, the different modelling approaches will be compared based on their predictive performance. The same evaluation framework will also be used to compare different biomarker specifications, including p-tau181, NfL, and a combination of the two biomarkers. For prognostic models predicting progression from MCI to AD dementia, predictions are most commonly made 2-4 years from baseline (Xia et al., 2025, p. 213). This reflects typical disease progression, where around one-third of individuals with MCI due to AD develop dementia within five years (Alzheimer’s Association, n.d.). Based on this, a landmark time of 1 year and prediction horizons of 2-6 years will be used to capture short- to mid-term progression. To ensure an unbiased assessment of model performance and generalisability, in-sample data will be used for model development with three quarters of the sample population, whilst out-of-sample data will be reserved for model evaluation with the remaining quarter.

The modelling approaches were chosen based on their methodological relevance and their ability to capture different aspects of the data, providing an overview of different approaches for modelling longitudinal biomarker data and survival outcomes. They will all be applied to data from the ADNI dataset, in accordance with its data use and access policies (ADNI, n.d.-b).

# Statistical Theory

## Survival Analysis

All of the modelling approaches considered in this study are grounded in the survival analysis framework. The primary aim is to predict the time until the occurrence of a pre-specified event of interest from some baseline time, usually the beginning of follow-up (Kleinbaum & Klein, 2012, p. 4). In this study, the event is defined as the first dementia diagnosis after baseline time, consistent with previous dementia survival studies (Park et al., 2019, p. 4). Diagnosis status, ptau-181 and NfL levels are all available at baseline.

Additionally, individuals with AD dementia are either considered as right censored, meaning that they do not reach the event during the follow-up period, or as interval censored, meaning that the exact date of the event is unknown (Kleinbaum & Klein, 2012, pp. 7, 286). Due to diagnostic exams being made either every half year or yearly, depending on the individuals cognition status and what stage of their protocol they are in, the exact date of transition to dementia can only be approximated. Therefore, participants in this study are truly interval censored, however they are not treated as such in order to allow for the use of the models of interest.

## Cox Proportional Hazards Model

To quantify the association between biomarkers and disease progression, relative hazards models are commonly used. These models compare the hazard of progression between individuals with different covariate profiles, and assume that their hazards are proportional.

Given that $T$ denotes either the time-to-event or the censuring time, the survival function models the probability of an individual remaining event-free up until time $t$, such that:

$$S(t) = Pr(T > t)$$

where the corresponding hazard function is given as the probability that the event occurs in the vicinity of time $t$ divided by the probability of being event-free at time $t$:

$$h(t) = \frac{f(t)}{S(t)} \quad \text{where} \quad f(t) = \frac{d}{dt} \left[1 - S(t) \right]$$

and $1 - S(t)$ is the cumulative risk function, $F(t)$ (Moore, 2016, pp. 11-14). The Lehmann alternative for comparing survival functions assumes that two survival functions, $S_0(t)$ and $S(t)$, are related such that:

$$S(t) = [S_0(t)]^{\psi}$$

where $\psi$ is the proportional hazards constant (Moore, 2016, pp. 43-44). This relationship can be re-expressed in terms of their hazard functions to give:

$$h(t) = \psi h_0(t)$$

which is the proportional hazards assumption (Moore, p. 55). Further, covariate information is linked to the proportional hazards constant exponentially, yielding the following model:

$$h(t) = h_0(t) exp\left\{ \mathbf{x}^T \boldsymbol{\beta} \right\}$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is a vector of covariates and $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is a vector of model parameters. In this study, the covariates of interest in the hazard model are age, gender, APOE-$\epsilon 4$ status and baseline values of p-tau181 and NfL. The latter two covariates are also included simultaneously, resulting in a multivariable Cox PH model.

### Model Assumptions

A key assumption of the Cox PH model is the assumed proportionality between hazard functions for different values of the specified covariates. This assumption is crucial for the construction of the partial likelihood, which allows the survival distribution to remain unspecified, since it allows the baseline hazard function to be dropped from the partial likelihood.

### Concordance Index

The concordance index ($C$ index) is an evaluation measure for the predictive performance of survival models. All pairs of individuals in the sample population are selected and the proportion of concordant pairs is evaluated. Pairs are said to be concordant if the individual with a higher cumulative risk, given by $F(t)$, has the shorter time-to-event (Park et al., 2021, p. 1701). The $C$ index will be considered as an initial evaluation metric for the different Cox PH models estimated in this study.

## Joint Modelling of Longitudinal and Survival Data

Joint models simultaneously model longitudinal and survival data, allowing for the coupling of a biomarker trajectory to some related survival outcome. In these models, the hazard function at time $t$ is directly dependent on the value of the longitudinal biomarker at time $t$. The biomarker process is modeled by a linear mixed-effects (LME) model whilst a Cox PH model describes the survival process.

### Linear Mixed-Effects Submodel

The longitudinal component of the joint model is specified by a LME model (**LAIRD & WAIRE**), capturing both population-level trends described by the fixed effects as well as individual variability, modeled by the random effects.

Since longitudinal data consists of repeated measurements from the same individuals, the assumption of independence between observations is illogical. In this analysis, the levels of p-tau181 and NfL for an individual at a specific time point, $t$, are correlated with measurements made on prior and subsequent occasions. Therefore, responses from an individual are expected to be more highly correlated than those between individuals. The modelling of this type of data, which can be considered grouped with non-independence within groups, is handled well by LME models.

Following the notation of Rizopoulos (2012, p. 54), the biomarker processes are modeled such that:

$$ y_i(t) = m_i(t) + \epsilon_i(t) \qquad \epsilon_i(t) \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\epsilon}) $$

$$ m_i(t) = \mathbf{X_i^T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{Z_i}^T\mathbf{b_i} \qquad \mathbf{b_i}(t) \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\mathbf{b}}) $$

where $y_i(t)$ is the observed biomarker measurement at time $t$ for the $i^{th}$ individual. Assuming that the true biomarker value is not observed due to measurement and other errors, $m_i(t)$ is the trajectory function which represents the true unobserved value of the biomarker at time $t$ for the $i^{th}$ individual. The fixed effects are described by $\mathbf{X_i}^T(t)\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and the random effects by $\mathbf{Z_i}^T\mathbf{b_i}$, where $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ are population-specific parameters and $\mathbf{b}_i$ are subject-specific parameters (Verbeke & Molenberghs, 2000, p. 23). These subject-specific parameters handle the observed dependence between repeated measurements. Combining the latent biomarker trajectory function with the error term gives:

$$ y_i(t) = \mathbf{X_i^T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{Z_i}^T\mathbf{b_i} + \epsilon_i(t) \qquad \mathbf{b_i}(t) \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\mathbf{b}}), \quad \epsilon_i(t) \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{\epsilon}) $$

### The Joint Model

The LME and Cox PH models are linked by a specified association structure. This structure can link the survival process to the current model estimate of the biomarker, $m_i(t)$, and the current rate of change of the biomarker trajectory, $m'_i(t)$. If both the current value and current rate of change are specified in the proportional hazards model, this becomes:

$$h(t|M_i, \mathbf{v_i}) = h_0(t)exp\left\{\boldsymbol{\gamma}^T\mathbf{w}_i + \alpha_1 m_i(t) + \alpha_2 m_i'(t) \right\}$$

$$\text{where }\qquad M_i = \left\{m_i,  0 \le s \le t\right\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad m_i'(t) = \frac{\delta} {\delta t} m_i(t)$$

In this formulation, $M_i$ represents the true unobserved biomarker profile up to time $t$, and the association parameters $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ link $m_i(t)$ and $m_i'(t)$ to the hazard function respectively. Further, $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ is a vector of log-hazard ratios and $\mathbf{w}_i$ is a vector of time-independent covariates for the $i^{th}$ individual.

This univariate framework is applied to longitudinal p-tau181 and NfL measurements separately to model their trajectories jointly with survival outcomes. This study will then apply multivariate JMs to simultaneously model both biomarkers and link their trajectories to the shared survival process describing progression to dementia due to AD.

**Both p-tau181 and NfL are considered simultaneously, as they capture complementary aspects of neurodegeneration and Alzheimer-related pathology (SOURCE). Ignoring their correlation may lead to biased estimation (Xu, 2021, p. 6)**

### Model Assumptions

A core assumption of the joint model for longitudinal and survival data is full conditional independence between the longitudinal outcome and the survival outcome. All dependence is assumed to be explained by the random effects, resulting in independence of the longitudinal and survival outcomes and the repeated biomarker measurements are independent of each other (Rizopolos, 2012, pp. 62-63).

### Estimation: Frequentist vs Bayesian Approach

The primary estimation approach that has been proposed for joint models is (semiparametric) maximum likelihood (Rizopoulos, 2012, p. 62). However, a key difficulty in joint modelling is that the estimation process can be very computationally demanding and may sometimes be infeasible (Wu et al., 2008).

A Bayesian alternative treats parameters as random variables and combines prior distributions with observed data to obtain posterior distributions, in contrast to the frequentist view where parameters are fixed but unknown (Carlin & Louis, 2008). This approach can simplify inference in complex models, and with weakly informative priors, it often yields results similar to maximum likelihood estimation (Brown & Ibrahim., 2003, p. 222).

Using the R package $JMbayes2$, joint models can be fitted via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms (Rizopoulos, 2018). MCMC generates dependent samples from the posterior distribution using a Markov chain, where each step depends only on the current state. As the chain evolves, its distribution converges to its stationary distribution, allowing the generated samples to be treated as representative of the posterior distribution and used for inference via Monte Carlo integration (Hamra et al., 2013, p. 628).

The package uses weakly informative priors, allowing stable estimation while letting the data primarily drive inference. The framework also accommodates multivariate settings, by introducing additional association parameters and regularising priors to handle higher-dimensional parameter structures (Rizopoulos, 2018).

### The Gelman-Rubin Statistic

Within Bayesian joint modelling, convergence of the Markov chains can be assessed by examining whether the parameters have stabilised over iterations, for example through trace plots. Additionally, it can be assessed by running multiple chains with different starting values and comparing within-chain and between-chain variability, which is formalized by the Gelman–Rubin statistic, $R$ (Peng, 2022).

Consider $J$ Markov chains, each with samples $x_1^{(j)}, x_2^{(j)}, \dots$ from the $j^{th}$ chain. For each chain, remove the first $D$ samples as “burn-in” and retain the following $L$ samples: $x_D^{(j)}, x_{D+1}^{(j)}, \dots, x_{D+L-1}^{(j)}$. One common choice is to set $D = L$.

Then calculate the chain mean for each chain,

$$\bar{x}_j = \frac{1}{L} \sum_{t=1}^{L} x_t^{(j)}$$

the overall mean across all chains (the grand mean),

$$\bar{x}_\cdot = \frac{1}{J} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \bar{x}_j$$

the between-chain variance,

$$B = \frac{L}{J-1} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \left(\bar{x}_j - \bar{x}_\cdot\right)^2$$

the within-chain variance for each chain,

$$s_j^2 = \frac{1}{L-1} \sum_{t=1}^{L} \left(x_t^{(j)} - \bar{x}_j\right)^2$$

and finally, the average within-chain variance,

$$W = \frac{1}{J} \sum_{j=1}^{J} s_j^2$$

Subsequently, the Gelman-Rubin statistic is:

$$R = \frac{\frac{L-1}{L} W + \frac{1}{L} B}{W}$$

As the number of iterations $L$ increases and the between-chain variation $B$ decreases, $R$ approaches 1. Thus, chains are typically run until $R$ is near this number. Being a unit-free ratio, $R$ provides a convenient summary of convergence without requiring specification of a particular parameter, making it a practical tool for monitoring MCMC chains before any inference is made (Peng, 2022).

## Joint Latent Class Mixed Model

JLCMMs address suspected disease heterogenity by assuming that the sample population consists of a finite number of unobserved subgroups (latent classes), each characterized by distinct longitudinal trajectories and survival risks (Kyheng et al., 2025, p. 2). Individuals within latent classes are assumed to share longitudinal biomarker trajectories and survival risks (Proust-Lima et al., 2018, p. 5) and the classes are not described by the observed covariates (Rizopoulos, 2012, p. 122).

In this analysis, univariate JLCMMs will be fit on the longitudinal p-tau181 and NfL measurements separately to assess whether any latent classes can be distinguished, and to ascertain any differences in predictive performance of these biomarkers.

### Class Submodel

The JLCMM consists of three submodels; a multinomial logistic submodel, a LME submodel and a proportional hazards submodel. Multinomial logistic regression models classes such that:

$$\pi_{i,g} = Pr(c_i = g | \mathbf{X}_i) = \frac{e^{\mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_g}}{\sum^{G}_{l = 1}e^{\mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_l}}$$

where $\mathbf{X}_i$ is the set of covaritates for the $i^{th}$ individual and $\boldsymbol{\beta}_g$ is the set of coefficients for the $g^{th}$ group. Given there are no prior assumptions about the latent classes, no covariates are specified in the multinomial logistic regression model (Kyheng et al., 2025, p. 2). The class submodel then simplifies to:

$$\pi_{i,g} = Pr(c_i = g) = \frac{e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0,g}}}{\sum^{G}_{l = 1}e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0,l}}}$$

where $\pi_{i,g}$ is the probability that the $i^{th}$ individual belongs to latent class $g$. Linking the class submodel to the longitudinal submodel and the survival submodel, assuming only a random intercept, results in the following:

$$h(t | c_i = g) = h_{0, g}(t)exp\left\{\boldsymbol{\gamma}^T\mathbf{w}_i + \alpha_1 m_i(t) \right\} $$

### Model Assumptions

In JLCMM, the biomarker and the time-to-event are considered to be conditionally independent given the latent classes, where all correlation between repeated measures of the biomarker is handled by the random effects in the longitudinal model (Proust-Lima et al., 2018, p. 122). This is in contrast to regular joint models, where the biomarker and time-to-event are assumed to be conditionally independent given the random effects (Proust-Lima et al., p. 62-63). The conditional independence assumptions for the JLCMM are as follows;

1.  Correlations between observations of the longitudinal biomarker are modeled by the random effects, $b_i$, in the longitudinal model.

2.  The relationship between biomarker trajectory and the time-to-diagnosis is captured completely by the latent class indicator, $c_i$.

There are various methods for assessing the conditional independence assumption, but simulations have demonstrated the superior performance of the score-test statistic in evaluating residual independence between the longitudinal and survival processes, even against two misspecified alternative hypotheses (Jacqmin-Gadda et al., 2010, p. 17).

The score test assumes the null hypothesis of conditional independence, that is, all correlation between the biomarker trajectory and time-to-event is captured entirely by group membership. Given the class membership is known, there is assumed to be no remaining dependence between the biomarker response and the time-to-event response. Assuming a model with a current value association structure, the association parameter, $\alpha_1$, is assumed to be zero under the null hypothesis (Jacqmin-Gadda et al., p. 13), such that:

$$H_0: \alpha_1 = 0 \qquad H_A: \alpha_1 \ne 0$$

Under the null hypothesis, the score test statistic, $U$, is $\chi^2$ distributed with degrees of freedom equal to the number of shared random effects in the model (Proust-Lima et al., p. 8). A significant test statistic supports the alternative hypothesis that there is residual dependence between the biomarker and time-to-event responses.

### Estimation

The log-likelihood for the JLCMM is much more tractable than for the regular joint model (Rizopoulos, 2012, p. 123), making estimation less computationally demanding. Log-likelihood estimation for JLCMM involves summing over the latent classes (Proust-Lima et al., 2014, p. 5), which is computationally advantageous when compared with the estimation of s which require mathematical approximation through, for example, the previously defined MCMC algorithm, due to integration over the random effects. For JLCMM, the log-likelihood is maximised using an iterative Marquardt algorithm (Proust-Lima et al., 2017, p. 10).

The Marquardt algorithm used in estimating JLCMMs updates the vector of model parameters to be used for log-likelihood evaluation, $\theta_{G}$, such that for iteration $l + 1$:

$$\theta_{G}^{\ (l + 1)} =
\theta_{G}^{\ (l)} - \delta \left( \tilde{\mathbf{H}}^{\ (l)} \right)^{-1}
\nabla (\ell(\theta_{G}^{\ (l)}))
\quad \text{where} \quad
\nabla(\ell(\theta_{G}^{\ (l)})) = \frac{\delta}{\delta\theta} \ell(\theta_{G}^{\ (l)})$$

where $\mathbf{H}$ is the Hessian matrix for parameter values for the $l^{th}$ iteration and, by default, $\delta$ equals $1$ but is updated to ensure improvement in the log-likelihood at each iteration (Proust-Lima et al., 2017, p.10). If necessary, the algorithm inflates the diagonal terms in the Hessian, producing $\tilde{\mathbf{H}}$, in order to ensure the next iteration produces an improved log-likelihood. According to Proust-Lima et al. (2017, p.10 ), this method is an update on the Newton-Raphson estimation algorithm that increases convergence rate and speed. It should be considered that there may be several local maxima, meaning the algorithm should be run several times using different starting values (Proust-Lima et al., 2014, p. 5).

In the $lcmm$ package developed by Proust-Lima et al. for estimating JLCMMs, a Weibull baseline hazard model is estimated by default and it is not possible to estimate a Cox PH model, in order to stay in the full-likelihood framework (Proust-Lima et al., 2014, p. 5). Therefore, it is necessary to assess whether the hazard is better modeled by the Weibull or a flexible baseline hazard model.

### Class Enumeration

Determining the number of latent classes (class enumeration) is one of the challenges of model selection for JLCMMs. Likelihood ratio tests cannot be performed for nested latent class models with differing number of classes, as regularity conditions which ensure a $\chi^2$ distributed test statistic do not hold (Celeux & Soromenho, 1996, p. 196). Therefore, other metrics must be utilised for this purpose.

One aspect of determining the optimal number of classes is minimization of the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), which is the preferred criterion for mixture models (Proust-Lima et al., 2014, p. 7). Classes must also be adequately discriminated, which is assessed by analysis of posterior class membership probabilities, given by (Proust-Lima et al., 2014, p. 7):

$$\widehat\pi_{i,g} = P(c_i = g |Y_i, (T^*_i, E_i); \widehat\theta_G) \\
= \frac{
\widehat\pi_{i,g}f(Y_i | c_i=g; \widehat\theta_G)\lambda_i(T_i | c_i=g; \widehat\theta_G)S_i(T_i | c_i=g; \widehat\theta_G)
}
{
\sum_{l = 1}^{G} \widehat\pi_{i,l}f(Y_i | c_i=l; \widehat\theta_G)\lambda_i(T_i | c_i=l; \widehat\theta_G)S_i(T_i | c_i=l; \widehat\theta_G)}$$

Reporting the proportion of individuals who have a posterior probability over a certain threshold (Proust-Lima et al., 2014, p. 7) - typically 0.7, 0.8 or 0.9 - illustrates the ability of the model to discriminate classes from one another. Mean posterior probabilities for each class can also be reported, with $\mu(\widehat\pi_g)$ values close to 0.5 showing poor class discrimination. Class sizes are also important, as classes that are made up of less than $5\%$ of the total sample population may be driven by outliers and therefore not be clinically meaningful.

**Entropy**

One possible measure of the discriminative power of a latent class structure is relative entropy (Ramaswamy et al., 1993 in Morgan et al., 2016, p. 150), which takes values between 0 and 1 and is calculated as follows:

$$EN(G) = 1 - 
\frac{
\sum_{i = 1}^{N}\sum_{g = 1}^{G} \widehat\pi_{i,g}log(\widehat\pi_{i,g})
}
{
Nlog(G)
}$$

where $G$ is the number of latent classes specified by the model and $\widehat\pi_{i,g}$ is the posterior probability that the $i^{th}$ individual belongs to class $g$. Relative entropy values closer to 1 demonstrate good discriminative ability of the model, where, for one class latent models, $EN(1) = 1$.

In addition to fulfilling the requirements for minimised BIC and maximised entropy, the chosen classes should be clinically meaningful. Analysis of the distribution of covariates by class can help elucidate the nature of the estimated latent classes.

## Evaluation of Predictive Performance

Information criteria such as the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) are often used to evaluate predictive performance in JMs combining longitudinal and survival data. However, when the main focus is the survival outcome and how well a longitudinal biomarker predicts it, performance is typically assessed using two main approaches: calibration, which measures how closely predicted probabilities agree with observed outcomes, and discrimination, which evaluates how well the model distinguishes between individuals who experience the event earlier versus later (Rizopoulos, 2012, p. 194). Time-dependent AUC is an example of a discrimination measure, while the time-dependent Brier score is a calibration-oriented measure that also reflects overall prediction error over time.

### Time-dependent AUC

ROC analysis is commonly used to evaluate the ability of a marker or model to discriminate between binary outcomes, such as diseased and non-diseased individuals (Zou et al., 2012, p. 3). However, the traditional ROC framework assumes that both disease status and marker values are fixed over time (Kamarudin et al., 2017, p. 1). In survival settings, this assumption is often violated, as event status changes during follow-up and marker values may vary over time. To account for this, time-dependent ROC curves have been developed, incorporating the timing of events and censoring, and providing a more appropriate framework for assessing prognostic accuracy (Kamarudin et al., 2017, p. 1). When a time-dependent framework is adopted, the disease status is evaluated at each time point, meaning that sensitivity and specificity may change over the course of the study.

Let $X_i$ represent the cumulative risk for the $i^{th}$ individual and let $D_i(t)$ denote the disease status at time $t$, where $D_i(t) = 1$ indicates presence of disease at time $t$, and $D_i(t) = 0$ otherwise (Kamarudin et al., 2017, p. 2). For a given threshold $c$, the time-dependent sensitivity and specificity, for time $t$, are then defined as:

$$ Se(c,t) = P(X_i > c \mid D_i(t) = 1) $$

$$ Sp(c,t) = P(X_i \le c \mid D_i(t) = 0) $$

where sensitivity refers to the probability of the model correctly detecting individuals who have experienced the event of interest before time $t$, whilst specificity is defined as the probability of the model correctly discerning individuals who remain event-free at time $t$.

Based on the definitions above, the corresponding receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve at a given time $t$, denoted by $ROC(t)$, can be constructed by plotting $Se(c,t)$ against $1 - Sp(c,t)$ across all possible thresholds (Kamarudin et al., 2017, p. 2).

The time-dependent AUC is then defined as:

$$ AUC(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} Se(c,t)\, d[1 - Sp(c,t)] $$

An AUC value of 1 means perfect ability to distinguish between patients with and without the condition, while an AUC of 0.5 means no discrimination at all, meaning the model performs no better than random guessing such as flipping a coin (Rizopoulos, 2012, p. 196)

### Time-dependent Brier Score

The Brier score can be thought of as the mean squared error of a prediction forecast. However, for survival data, the true event status cannot be known for censored individuals. Therefore, an inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting (IPCW) adjusted time-dependent Brier score has been formulated to account for bias due to censoring, where those with earlier event times are over-represented, leading to underestimation of survival probabilities (Prince et al., 2025, p. 4). IPCW weights are calculated for each individual $i = 1 , ... , n$ at each time point $t$, such that:

$$\omega_i(t) =
\frac{\mathbb{I} \left\{ T_i^*\le t, \delta_i = 1 \right\} }{G(T^*_i-)} +
\frac{\mathbb{I} \left\{ T_i^* > t \right\} }{G(t)}$$

where $G(t)$ is the censoring survival function, which quantifies the probability of surviving a censoring event, $T_i^* -$ is a time point infinitesimally smaller than the observed time $T_i^*$, and $\mathbb{I} \left\{ \cdot \right\}$ is an indicator function (Prince et al., 2025, pp. 4-5).

The commonly formulated Brier score:

$$\text{BS} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^{n }(Y_i(t) - \widehat S_i(t))^2$$

where $\widehat S_i(t)$ is the predicted survival probability for the $i^{th}$ individual at time $t$ and $Y_i(t)$ is their observed outcome at that time (Park et al., 2021, p. 1704) is insufficient for censored survival data. Adjusting for censoring, the IPCW-adjusted Brier score is given as:

$$BS =
\frac{1}{ \tilde n(t)}\sum_{i = 1}^{n} \left(
\frac{( \widehat S_i(t))^2 \mathbb{I} \left\{ T_i^*\le t, \delta_i = 1 \right\} }{G(T^*_i-)} +
\frac{ (1 - \widehat S_i(t))^2 \mathbb{I} \left\{ T_i^* > t \right\} }{G(t)}
\right)$$

where $\tilde n(t)$ is the sum of all IPCW weights at time $t$ (Prince et al., 2025, p. 6). The Brier score takes values from 0 to 1, where a score closer to 0 is given to a model with better predictive ability.

# Data

The data used in this analysis comes from the ADNI cohort under the ADNI1, ADNIGO and ADNI2 protocols. The variables of interest were all retrieved from the ADNIMERGE2 package, found in the ADNI database (ADNI, n.d.-b). In accordance with the ADNI leadership guidelines, which state that there were serious data quality concerns for individuals with a PTID in the format "381_S_10###" , checks were run to assure that no observations with these PTIDs were present in the data set (ADNI, 2026).

The inclusion criteria for this study required participants to have recorded diagnostic visits and longitudinal blood biomarker measurements of both p-tau181 and NfL. The exclusion criteria was any individual with a baseline diagnosis of dementia.

Moreover, the inclusion criteria also related to the number of biomarker measurements per individual and were set to at least three measurements. However, a common issue in modelling longitudinal biomarker data, namely whether to include or exclude individuals with sparse data in the analysis (Rizopoulos, 2012, pp. 27-28). While the previously described studies included all participants regardless of the number of measurements per individual, a study examining different cognitive biomarkers for predicting progression to AD included only those with at least three complete longitudinal cognitive assessments (Guo et al., 2026, p. 2). Other studies have restricted the inclusion criteria further to those with at least ten longitudinal biomarker measurements in order to ensure that the approximation did not lead to non-ignorable bias (Wang et al., 2024, pp. 591-592). Participants with cross-sectional data cannot provide information on within-subject change over time; however, they may still contribute useful information on between-subject variability (Fitzmaurice et al., 2011, pp. 214-215). Excluding individuals with sparse data may reduce precision and potentially introduce bias depending on the pattern and mechanism of missingness (Fitzmaurice et al., 2011, p. 491). Therefore, sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the results when including individuals with at least one biomarker measurement.

Application of these criteria yielded a sample of 704 participants with at least three biomarker measurements. Inclusion of participants with at least one biomarker measurement increased the sample size to 934.

All missing values were removed prior to the analysis to ensure a complete-case data set and avoid bias introduced by incomplete observations.

## Variables

### Diagnosis Status

The variable of primary interest represents three diagnostic states - cognitively normal (CN), MCI and dementia - and was retrieved from the DXSUM data set in ADNIMERGE2. Diagnostic status is assessed over several examination dates, with the number of diagnostic exams differing depending on the baseline diagnosis.

Since the study focuses on time to incident dementia, participants are classified as either non-demented or demented for the survival analyses, without distinguishing between CN and MCI states. Diagnostic records occurring more than 50 days prior to the first biomarker measurement were excluded to maintain temporal alignment between clinical and biomarker data.

The sample size of the in-sample data set was 528, among which 128 experienced the event of dementia, corresponding to 24.24%, while 400 individuals were censored. In the out-of-sample, there were 176 individuals, among whom 49 experienced the event of dementia, corresponding to 27.84%, while 127 individuals were censored. The corresponding sample sizes for the in-sample and out-of-sample data sets, as well as the numbers of events and censored participants when extending the study population to include individuals with at least one biomarker measurement, can be found in Appendix 8.1; Table 12 & 13. The corresponding distributions and summary statistics for the variables of interest are presented for this cohort in Appendix 8.1; Table 12 and are described below for participants with at least three measurements.

### p-tau181 and NfL

The p-tau181 measurements were retrieved from the UGOPTAU181 data set, which was processed by the University of Gothenburg (ADNI, n.d.-b), while the NfL measurements were retrieved from the BLENNOWPLASMANFLLONG data set, processed by the Blennow Lab (ADNI, n.d.-b). The unit of measurement is not specified in the data set documentation for either p-tau181 or NfL.

P-tau181 values ranged from 0.4 to 238.3, with a median of 15.5. Similarly, NfL values ranged from 6.9 to 408.0, with a median of 36.5. The pronounced right-skewness for both biomarkers was the basis for log-transformation in order to better satisfy the assumption of normality (Appendix 8.1; Figure 6a & 6b). Values exceeding three standard deviations from the mean were further examined and retained in the analysis, as they reflected consistent longitudinal patterns within individuals rather than implausible observations.

Here, it is also worth noting that the correlation between log-transformed p-tau181 and NfL was 0.34 (Appendix 8.1.4), indicating a weak positive association. This suggests that the biomarkers share some common variation while largely capturing distinct biological processes. Overall, this supports the use of a multivariate framework, as it allows their dependence to be accounted for while evaluating both their individual and combined associations with disease progression. Moreoever, they showed low to medium correlation with the other numerical covariates, indicating no major concerns regarding multicollinearity and suggesting that they are all suitable for inclusion in the models.

Biomarker examination dates ranged from 1 February 2007 to 6 June 2016, while diagnostic assessment dates spanned 29 September 2005 to 7 November 2025. In this analysis, baseline was defined as the first biomarker examination date, ensuring alignment of biomarker follow-up with dementia onset.

52 participants had two measurements with different values recorded on the same examination date. To ensure consistency, the mean value of these measurements was selected as the primary approach. Sensitivity analyses consisted of defining the measurements by their first and last measurement, respectively.

Furthermore, discrepancies were observed between the p-tau181 and NfL examination dates despite sharing the same visit code. Five cases exceeded 30 days, with differences of up to 231 days, indicating that these did not represent the same examination occasion. To address this, a harmonized examination date was constructed as the midpoint between the two biomarker examination dates. This date was used to define the baseline. An additional sensitivity analysis was conducted in which baseline was defined as the first examination date across biomarkers.

### Age

Additionally, age is included as a covariate when predicting progression to dementia, as risk of dementia is known to increase with age (Alzheimer’s Society, n.d.). The variable was retrieved from the PTDEMOG data set and was initially recorded as year of birth for each participant (ADNI, n.d.-b) which was transformed into age at baseline. Baseline age ranged from 55 to 94 years, with a median age of 74 years.

### Gender

Another covariate included when predicting progression to dementia is participants’ gender at birth, as recorded on their original birth certificate, due to reported differences in disease risk and progression between genders. More precisely, women aged over 80 have a slightly higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease compared to men of the same age (Alzheimer’s Society, n.d.). This binary variable includes two categories: male and female (ADNI, n.d.-b). Among the included participants, 315 were female, while 389 were male. As for age, the variable was retrieved from the PTDEMOG dataset.

### APOE4-status

Finally, APOE-$\epsilon 4$ status is included as a covariate when predicting progression to dementia, due to its well-established role as a genetic risk factor for AD. The $\epsilon 4$ allele of apolipoprotein E (APOE) increases the risk of AD, whereas the -$\epsilon 2$ allele has been shown to have a protective effect (Wong et al.). The variable was retrieved from the APOERES dataset (ADNI, n.d.-b). Initially coded numerically based on the number of $\epsilon 4$ alleles, the variable was recoded into three ordinal categories: 0 alleles (non-carriers), 1 allele (heterozygous carriers; 2/4 or 3/4), and 2 alleles (homozygous carriers; 4/4). 83 participants carried no APOE-$𝜀4$ alleles, 578 carried one allele, and 43 carried two alleles

# Results

## Model Fit Overview

### Cox PH Models

First, Cox PH models incorporating baseline values of p-tau181, NfL, or both biomarkers were estimated. Additional covariates were gender, age at baseline and APOE genotype. Initially, fitting the model with all levels of genotype - which denotes the specific APOE allele combination - resulted in non-significant coefficients for all levels. Therefore, genotype was collapsed into three levels denoting the presence of the APOE-$\epsilon 4$ allele, taking the following values: 0 alleles (non-carriers), 1 allele (heterozygous carriers; $\epsilon 2$/$\epsilon 4$ or $\epsilon 3$/$\epsilon 4$), and 2 alleles (homozygous carriers; $\epsilon 4$/$\epsilon 4$).

Prior to interpreting the predictive performance of the models, the proportional hazards assumption was assessed for all covariates to verify that the effects remained constant over time. Considering the Cox PH model is defined as the survival submodel in the subsequent JMs, it is critical this assumption is met in order to reliably evaluate the JMs. The resulting $p$-values are presented in Table 14 (Appendix 8.2).

At a 5% significance level, most covariates satisfied the proportional hazards assumption across all models, as indicated by non-significant $p$-values for gender, APOE-$ε4$ status, and the biomarker variables. However, age at baseline consistently showed significant $p$-values, indicating a violation of the assumption. The same pattern was observed for the GLOBAL test, which jointly evaluates the proportional hazards assumption across all covariates and is sensitive to covariate-specific departures from the assumption; it also yielded significant or borderline significant $p$-values.

Given this violation, age at baseline was excluded from the final Cox PH models. The refitted models yielded the $p$-values presented in Table 1.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "p-values for the proportional hazards assumption tests after exclusion of age at baseline in the Cox PH models"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/table_ph_final.rds"))
```

After excluding age at baseline, the GLOBAL test yielded $p$-values above the 5% significance level, no longer indicating any violation of the proportional hazards assumption. All other covariates also remained non-significant, suggesting that they jointly do not exhibit systematic time-dependent effects in any of the refitted models.

Furthermore, an initial comparison of model performance by assessment of the concordance indices for all Cox PH models was performed. The results presented in Table 2 show that the concordance index evaluates all three models similarly, with results indicating adequate discrimination.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "Concordance indices for the fitted Cox PH models with baseline biomarker values"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/c_index_table.rds"))
```

### Joint Models

Next, JMs that incorporated the longitudinal trajectories of p-tau181 and NfL with the time-to-diagnosis data were estimated. For the longitudinal component, an LME model was estimated separately for p-tau181 and NfL.

Plotting the residuals against the fitted values for the LME model with p-tau181 showed no clear evidence of heteroskedasticity, as shown in Appendix 8.3; Figure 8a. The slight deviations in the tails of the Q-Q plot were also not considered to be of concern (Appendix 8.3; Figure 8b). A similar pattern was observed for the LME model of NfL, where the plot of residuals against fitted values demonstrated even less evidence of heteroskedasticity compared to the corresponding plot for p-tau181 (Appendix 8.3; Figure 9a). The Q-Q plot for NfL showed similar results to those observed for p-tau181 (Appendix 8.3; Figure 9b). Generalised LME models with different link functions were also fit and their residuals analysed, however none of these models demonstrated a better fit than the LME models with log-transformed biomarker measurements. Consequently, these models were retained as the longitudinal submodels within the joint modelling framework.

The choice of random effects structure for the JMs was limited due to the $JMBayes2$ package currently only supporting those including a random slope. Therefore, all LME models were fit with a random intercept and slope. However, models with a simple structure with only a random intercept and an extended structure including a random slope were fit using maximum likelihood estimation in order to perform likelihood ratio tests. The results show that the extended structure was a better fit for NfL, but a simpler structure would have been preferable for p-tau181 (Appendix 8.2; Table 13).

Thus, JMs with a random intercept and slope were estimated for longitudinal measurements of p-tau181, NfL, or both simultaneously. For each model, three MCMC chains were used, with 11,000 iterations and 1,000 burn-in iterations for the univariate JMs, and 20,000 iterations with 2,000 burn-in iterations for the multivariate JM. To ensure convergence of the JMs, trace plots of the $\alpha$-parameters, which represent the associations between the longitudinal and survival submodels, were examined for each model. The evaluation started with the JM for p-tau181, presented in Figure 1.

![Traceplot of log-transformed p-tau181](figures/convergence_plot_ptau.png){#fig-converg-ptau}

The trace plot shows that the three MCMC chains fluctuate around a stable mean value throughout the iterations, without any clear trend or drift. This suggests that the chains have reached a stable region. In addition, the chains overlap well and mix with each other, indicating that they are sampling from the same posterior distribution. Although some random variation is present, this is expected in MCMC sampling. Overall, the plot supports good convergence.

A similar pattern was observed for the JM including NfL, as shown in Appendix 8.4; Figure 10a. The chains likewise fluctuate around a stable mean value with good mixing, indicating convergence of the $α$-parameters comparable to the JM including p-tau181.

Finally, the multivariate JM also exhibited a similar overall behaviour (Appendix 8.4; Figure 10b-c). Compared to the single-biomarker models, however, the trace plot for the multivariate JM shows a slightly wider range of $α$-values, indicating a somewhat larger variability in the $α$-parameters. This suggests increased uncertainty in the parameter estimates, which is expected given the higher complexity of the model. Despite this, the chains still fluctuate around a stable mean value with no visible trend or drift, and they continue to overlap and mix well. Thus, all three models appear to have converged adequately.

Additionally, convergence of the models was assessed by examining the $\widehat{R}$ values of the survival outcome and the longitudinal outcome in each joint model, with the survival $\widehat{R}$ values presented in Table 3.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "$\\widehat{\\mathbf{R}}$ values of the survival outcome in the joint models"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/rhat_survival_table.rds"))
```

The $\widehat{R}$ values for the survival outcomes remained very close to 1 across all JMs. This indicates good convergence of the MCMC chains for these components and confirms the convergence patterns observed in the $α$-parameter trace plots, with no evidence of convergence issues.

While Table 3 presents the $\widehat{R}$ values for the survival outcomes, the corresponding $\widehat{R}$ values for the longitudinal outcomes in each JM are shown in Table 4.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "$\\widehat{\\mathbf{R}}$ values of the longitudinal outcome in the joint models"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/rhat_longitudinal_table.rds"))
```

In a similar manner, the $\widehat{R}$ values for the longitudinal outcomes are generally close to 1 across all JMs. When considered together with the trace plots and survival $\widehat{R}$ values, the results support adequate convergence of the models.

### Joint Latent Class Mixed Models

Finally, JLCMMs were estimated. The models were selected via comparison of BIC and entropy as well as assessment of posterior probabilities and classifications for models with up to four latent classes. An intercept only random effects structure was chosen due to minimised BIC for all models. A Weibull baseline hazard was chosen and checked against whether a flexible baseline hazard with the same number of parameters resulted in a lower BIC, which was the case for all models. The results of each model were verified using the $gridsearch()$ function which allows for better exploration of the parameter space to ensure finding the global instead of a local maximum solution. This check confirmed that using random starts from the one class model was sufficient for finding the global maximum for all models.

The log-likelihood, BIC and entropy of the models using longitudinal p-tau181 measurements are presented below (Table 5). Log-likelihood and entropy increased with additional latent classes, however the BIC was minimised for the model with two latent classes.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Log-likelihood, BIC and entropy for JLCMMs with longitudinal p-tau181 measurements"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/summary_jlcmm_ptau.rds"))
```

Posterior classifications show the number of individuals assigned to each class, whereas the mean posterior probabilities show, for individuals in each class, the average probability of being assigned to each class. For example, values for $class1$, $prob1$ close to $1$ and $class2$, $prob1$ close to $0$ show good class discrimination.

For the two class model (Table 6), the class sizes are reasonable and the mean posterior probabilities show good class discrimination, meaning the model has high certainty in assigning individuals to their respective classes. Comparison with the three class model (Table 7) shows somewhat poorer class discrimination as well as a questionably small $class3$, with only $3.79\%$ of individuals being assigned to this class.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior classification table and mean posterior probabilities for the two class JLCMM for longitudinal p-tau181 measurements"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/pprob_m1_ptau.rds"))
```

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior classification table and mean posterior probabilities for the three class JLCMM for longitudinal p-tau181 measurements"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/pprob_m2_ptau.rds"))
```

The score test statistic for the conditional independence assumption was significant for the one class model ($50.336, p < 0.001$) but became non-significant ($0.122, p = 0.727$) upon modelling two latent classes, further evidence that the data supports two latent classes in the sample population. All model parameters were significant ($p < 0.001$) and are presented in Table 16 (Appendix 8.5). Therefore, the two class model was chosen for this analysis.

The log-likelihood, BIC and entropy provided in Table 8 for candidate models using longitudinal NfL data suggest that also in this instance the two class model provided the best fit for the data and had the highest classification certainty. Log-likelihood increased most between the one class and the two class model, whilst only a slight increase was exhibited between the two and three class models. BIC was minimised and entropy was maxmised for the two class model.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Log-likelihood, BIC and entropy for JLCMMs with longitudinal NfL measurements"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/summary_jlcmm_nfl.rds"))
```

Class sizes were reasonable and good class discrimination was shown when assessing the average posterior probabilities (Table 9). The one class model had a significant score test statistic ($33.409, p < 0.001$) which became non-significant for the two class model ($0.368, p = 0.544$). The two class model was therefore chosen.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior classification table and mean posterior probabilities for the two class JLCMM for longitudinal NfL measurements"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/pprob_m1_nfl.rds"))
```

The distribution of age at baseline, gender, APOE-$\epsilon 4$ status, and baseline biomarker values for each class estimated from the JLCMM using longitudinal p-tau181 measurements are displayed in Appendix 8.6; Table 10. For the continuous variables, median values as well as first and third quartiles are reported. For the categorical variables, raw values as well as percentage of individuals per class are given. Appendix 8.6; Table 11 presents the same results for the JLCMM estimated for longitudinal NfL measurements. The results show that both models estimate a high-risk and a low-risk class, where the high-risk class has higher median values for both biomarker baselines and age, as well as a higher proportion of those with two APOE-$\epsilon 4$ alleles than the low-risk class. The class-specific survival curves are found in Appendix 8.6; Figure 10.

## Model Comparison

In order to compare the predictive performance of the different modelling approaches, the time-dependent AUC for each model was calculated at yearly time points from a landmark time of one year over horizons of one to five years. Figure 2 provides the time-dependent AUC of the different models across all prediction horizons, with the biomarker fixed as p-tau181.

![Time-Dependent AUC (p-tau181)](figures/q1_auc_ptau.png){#fig-auc-ptau}

Among these models, the time-dependent AUC curves remain consistently high, with values exceeding 0.75 for all horizons, regardless of modelling approach. This indicates that the models demonstrate stable and relatively strong discriminative ability in distinguishing between individuals who progressed to AD dementia and those who did not over time. The values are slightly higher for earlier predictions, especially for the JM. Differences between the models decrease over time, resulting in increasingly similar curves, yet the AUC values suggest that the best predictions made at year six were from the JLCMM. The Cox PH model consistently yields the lowest AUC values.

Among the models incorporating NfL, a similar overall pattern is observed. As shown in Appendix 8.6; Figure 11a, the curves remain at comparable levels to those seen for the p-tau181 models, with time-dependent AUC values exceeding 0.75 across all horizons. For earlier predictions, where the values are slightly higher across models, the JM once again yields the highest AUC values. These values then decline over time, becoming more similar to those of the other models. In addition, it shows a slightly higher value for the JLCMM at for the latest prediction horizon.

Appendix 8.6; Figure 11b presents the models incorporating both biomarkers simultaneously, demonstrating higher AUC values for early predictions made using the JM. These values gradually decline over time, yielding values more similar to those of the Cox PH model for later predictions.

These results are also indicated by Table 10 which contains the AUC values for each modelling approach and at each horizon.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "Time-dependent AUC by model and prediction time point"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/results_table_AUC.rds"))
```

For instance, by showing that the JM among the p-tau181-based models has an AUC value of 0.902 for predictions made at year two, while the Cox PH model has an AUC value of 0.823 and the JLCMM has an AUC value of 0.862, Table 10 confirms the results previously observed in the figure. The differences between the models then decrease over time; for predictions at four years, the AUC values are 0.802 for the Cox PH model, 0.806 for the JM, and 0.811 for the JLCMM.

When evaluating the models' predictive performances using time-dependent Brier scores instead, the same overall patterns are observed, with the key difference that lower values, and therefore lower curves, indicate better predictive performance. Figure 3 presents the time-dependent Brier score curves for the different modelling approaches, with the biomarker specification fixed to p-tau181.

![Time-dependent Brier scores (p-tau181)](figures/q1_brier_ptau.png){#fig-brier-ptau}

Among the models incorporating p-tau181, the time-dependent Brier score curves remain consistently low, across all modelling approaches, although they show a slight increase over time. This suggests stable overall predictive accuracy and relatively low prediction error for progression to AD dementia. However, the curve for the Cox PH model curve remain slightly higher than the curves representing the JM and the JLCMM models, meaning that it consistently yields higher Brier scores than the two other models. More precisely, the AUC for this model range from approximately 0.05 for early predictions to 0.17 for late predictions, while the corresponding AUC for the other models range from approximately 0.02 to 0.16. In other terms, two other curves remain closely aligned, although the curve for the JM is slightly lower at the two year-follow-up, indicating a slightly better predictive performance at this time-point.

This pattern holds for the models incorporating NfL (Appendix 8.6; Figure 12a). The curves remain consistently high, at around the same AUC range as the curves representing the models incorporating p-tau181. At the same time, the curve for the Cox PH model remain slightly higher than the curves representing the curves for the JM and the JLCMM, indicating a worse predictive performance.

The same can be said for the time-dependent Brier scores among the models incorporating both biomarkers simultaneously. Appendix 8.6; Figure 12b demonstrates that the JM and the JLCMM yield similar, stable AUC values across all prediction horizons, ranging from approximately 0.02 at earlier predictions to 0.16 at later horizons.

Table 11 presents the Brier scores for each modelling approach and at each horizon.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "Time-dependent Brier score by model and prediction time point"
kable_standard(readRDS("tables/results_table_Brier.rds"))
```

For predictions at two years, the Cox PH incorporating p-tau181 achieves an AUC value of 0.054, which is notably higher than the corresponding AUC values for the JM and JLCMM incorportating p-tau181, which yield AUC values of 0.018 and 0.024, respectively. This indicates that the Cox PH model perform the worst, with the JLCMM coming in second and the JM performing the best. The same results are observed among the models incorporating NfL, as well as among those incorporating both biomarkers.

## Biomarker Comparison

The models' performances in predicting progression to AD dementia were also examined in order to compare the different biomarker specifications, meaning modelling either using p-tau181, NfL or a combination of the two biomarkers. Figure 4 illustrates how the time-dependent AUC of the models changes with biomarker specification across prediction horizons, with the model being fixed as Cox PH.

![Time-dependent AUC (Cox PH)](figures/q2_auc_cox.png){#fig-auc-cox}

Among the Cox PH models, the model incorporating NfL shows slightly higher time-dependent AUC values overall than the model incorporating p-tau181 across the follow-up period. However, both single-marker models are consistently outperformed by the combined model, indicating superior discriminative ability in distinguishing between individuals who progress to AD dementia and those who do not over time.

Within the JM framework, a similar overall pattern is observed. Appendix 8.7; Figure 13a demonstrates that the multivariate JM provides the strongest predictive performance across all horizons, with consistently higher AUC values than the univariate models. Nevertheless, the NfL-based model generally shows slightly higher values than the p-tau181-based model.

Comparing JLCMMs, NfL consistently shows slightly higher AUC values than the model including p-tau181, except for predictions made at the three-year point, where the p-tau181 model shows a slightly higher value (Appendix 8.7; Figure 13b).

The time-dependent AUC values for each biomarker specification at each horizon are also presented in Table 10. For example, for predictions made two years from baseline, the multivariate JM achieved an AUC value of 0.967, compared to 0.953 for the NfL model and 0.902 for the p-tau181 model. This indicates that the multivariate model provides the highest predictive performance at this time point.

When observing the time-dependent Brier score curves, such as Figure 5 presenting the curves for the Cox PH models, a similar pattern can be observed, although not as evident.

![Time-Dependent Brier scores (Cox PH)](figures/q2_brier_cox.png){#fig-brier-cox}

All three Cox PH models yield low and similar time-dependent Brier scores across all horizons, as reflected by the closely aligned curves. For predictions made at year six, the curve for the model incorporating both biomarkers simultaneously is slightly lower, indicating a lower Brier score and thus better overall predictive accuracy at this time point compared to the two single-marker models.

In a similar manner, the multivariate JM demonstrates lower AUC compared to the corresponding models incorporating solely p-tau181 or NfL (Appendix 8.7; Figure 14a). These two models consistently show similar AUC values, a pattern that is also observed for the JLCMMs incorporating p-tau181 or NfL, respectively (Appendix 8.7; Figure 14b).

Table 11, containing the time-dependent Brier scores for each biomarker specification and at each horizon, also confirms this pattern. For instance, for all three Cox PH models, predictions made two years ahead yield values ranging from 0.052 to 0.054, indicating minimal differences in predictive performance at this time point. For predictions made six years ahead, the differences between models becomes slightly more pronounced: modelling baseline values for both biomarkers yields a value of 0.142 at this horizon, whilst the models with baseline p-tau181 and NfL as covariates yield values of 0.158 and 0.159, respectively.

## Sensitivity Analyses

To examine the robustness of the results, several sensitivity analyses were performed.

First, for individuals with two biomarker measurements reported for the same date and visit code, the analysis was run using the first or last recorded value instead of their average. The majority of the time-dependent AUC and Brier scores values were identical to those in the main analysis, with any differences being minimal at approximately 0.010. This indicates that the results were robust to the handling of duplicated measurements.

A second sensitivity analysis related to the difference in time between the examinations of p-tau181 and NfL. Instead of defining the baseline date as the midpoint between the differing biomarker examination dates, it was defined as the earlier of the two biomarker examination dates. The Cox PH models still consistently yielded the lowest AUC values across modelling approaches, while the performance of the JMs and the JLCMMs varied across follow-up points and biomarker specifications. Additionally, the models incorporating both biomarkers still performed the best overall, yielding the highest AUC values and lowest Brier scores across the follow-up period.

In response to the debate over whether individuals with sparse data should be included when modelling longitudinal trajectories, all models were also estimated on an extended cohort of individuals with one or more p-tau181 and NfL measurements. Compared with the analysis restricted to participants with at least three biomarker measurements, the relative performance of the JMs and JLCMMs decreased, particularly compared to Cox PH models, which remained stable and in some cases showed similar or higher AUC values. In contrast, Brier scores showed that Cox models generally had worse calibration than the JMs and JLCMMs. Both metrics indicate that models based on p-tau181 alone performed similarly to, or in some cases better than, models including both biomarkers. NfL consistently displayed the lowest values across this sensitivity analysis.

Finally, to address the interval censored nature of the data, event times were defined as the midpoint between diagnostic exams when a positive dementia diagnosis was given. For all models, both discrimination and calibration were poorer than in the main analysis, with the largest differences in AUC observed for JMs and JLCMMs. The differences between Brier scores from the main analysis and this sensitivity analysis were relatively similar across models, with differences in both AUC and Brier scores levelling out over prediction horizons. These results show that this method is a worse approximation than defining event times as the diagnostic exam dates for this cohort.

# Discussion

## Main Findings and Conclusions

This study compared the predictive performance of different modelling frameworks for time-to-diagnosis in individuals from the ADNI cohort with dementia as the event of interest, structured across three levels of information and their corresponding model approaches. At the most basic level, baseline biomarker information was used in Cox PH models estimated with either p-tau181 or NfL, or both simultaneously. The second level incorporated longitudinal biomarker information by extending these Cox PH models within a joint modelling framework, accounting for repeated measurements over time. The most complex level combined longitudinal biomarker trajectories with latent class structure using the JLCMM framework to capture heterogeneity in disease progression by modelling class-specific trajectories and survival processes. For both JLCMMs, a two class model was determined to best model the data. These models estimated one high-risk class and one low-risk class. All reported models were adjusted for gender and APOE-$ε4$ status.

The predictive performance of these models was assessed by comparing time-dependent AUC and Brier scores with a landmark time of 1 year over horizons spanning 1-5 years. Both evaluations demonstrated that all three modelling approaches showed relatively good predictive performance in terms of both discriminative ability and overall predictive accuracy, with AUC values above 0.75 and Brier scores below approximately 0.15 across all horizons.

At the same time, the time-dependent AUC showed that the predictive performance differed across the three levels of information considered. Overall, incorporating longitudinal biomarker trajectories improved discriminatory ability compared to baseline only measurements. This improvement was consistent across biomarkers (p-tau181, NfL, and their combination) and was most pronounced for early predictions, where JMs achieved the highest AUC values relative to the Cox PH models. These findings are consistent with those of Goksuluk et al. (2025, p. 14), who, in the context of mortality risk prediction in peritoneal dialysis patients, reported improved predictive performance of joint modelling approaches compared to Cox PH models using, among other specifications, baseline biomarker values.

The difference between JMs and the other models were more pronounced at earlier time horizons, suggesting that JMs may offer better discrimination and calibration. This is clinically meaningful, as identification of those at risk of progression to AD dementia in the near future is beneficial, for example in determining individuals best placed for clinical trial enrollment. However, JLCMMs achieved comparable or higher AUC values at intermediate to longer horizons, indicating that these models may have value for predictions made further into the future. This indicates that there is no single modelling approach that consistently dominates in terms of time-dependent AUC across all time horizons.

The corresponding time-dependent Brier scores presented a consistent but complementary pattern. The JMs and the JLCMMs generally achieved better predictive accuracy compared to the Cox PH models over intermediate and longer horizons, reflecting better overall calibration when longitudinal information was incorporated. The difference between these two modelling approaches, however, remained small, as similarly shown by the time-dependent AUC.

Goksuluk et al. (2025, p. 11) reported that models including multiple biomarkers simultaneously performed slightly better than models including a single biomarker, which is also supported by the findings of Yuan et al., who investigated joint models incorporating p-tau181 and NfL, as well as by the findings of the present study. Across all modelling approaches, the combination of p-tau181 and NfL provided the best overall predictive performance for progression to AD dementia compared to either biomarker alone. This was evident in both discrimination and calibration. For predictions made two years from baseline, NfL displayed higher AUC values accross all three modelling approaches, suggesting short-term longitudinal NfL data may have better discriminative ability than p-tau181. Brier scores for predictions over all horizons were broadly comparable, without a consistent advantage of one biomarker over the other, indicating that neither biomarker alone fully captures the available prognostic information. Instead, the two biomarkers appear to provide complementary information, with p-tau181 reflecting AD specific pathology and NfL capturing more general neurodegenerative processes. When combined, they improved both the ranking of individuals according to risk and the accuracy of absolute risk predictions.

Sensitivity analyses showed however that including participants with only one biomarker measurement substantially reduced the performance of the JMs and the JLCMMs. While this reduction may partly reflect differences in sample size and number of events after inclusion of participants sparse data, the relatively stable Cox PH models suggest that reduced longitudinal information was likely the main contributing factor. This further indicates that the predictive benefit of the longitudinal approaches depends on sufficient repeated biomarker measurements. Additionally, the reduced performance of combined biomarker models indicates that the added value of NfL depends on the availability of sufficient longitudinal information.

## Further Research

Diagnostic exam dates were used as a proxy for AD onset in this analysis despite the exact time of dementia onset is unknown and individuals being interval censored. This has the potential to introduce bias in the estimated event times, as the time-to-diagnosis is overestimated. Despite this, interval censoring was not adequately accounted for given the level of this thesis and its time constraints. This would require more complex statistical methods, for which standard Cox PH models would no longer be directly applicable. Results from the sensitivity analysis support this suggestion, as crudely estimating event times was proven to reduce overall predictive performance. As a direction for future research, it is therefore recommended that progression to dementia be modeled using interval censored survival methods in order to reduce potential bias and better reflect the underlying disease process.

Additionally, an issue with this analysis is that it did not compare a multivariate JLCMM modelling both p-tau181 and NfL measurements, due to time constraints. Currently, the $lcmm$ package does not offer dynamic predictions for multivariate JLCMMs, meaning there would be a heavier time burden were this model to be included. The predictive performance for the different biomarker specifications were subsequently not compared in a complete manner within this modelling approach. Therefore, further research could work to assess the benefit in class-specific modelling of these biomarkers simultaneously. From the results of this analysis, the JLCMMs appeared to offer better late predictions, and further work could be done to assess whether the performance of these models diverges further over longer horizons.

Finally, as blood-based biomarker research is still emerging, rich longitudinal data sets for these biomarkers remain limited. For example, individuals in the data used for this analysis had at most five biomarker measurements. Future studies should therefore aim to replicate and extend this analysis once longitudinal biomarker data is available over longer time frames or cohorts with more frequent longitudinal sampling become available. This would improve the precision of both trajectory estimation and the assessment of associations between biomarker dynamics and disease progression.

## Residual Diagnositics
